title: X-chromosome inactivation draws L1 mutagenesis to the human X chromosome.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Opened the Zenodo deposit (10.5281/zenodo.20175115): it holds exactly three Python scripts (3.6 kB, 1.9 kB, 7.2 kB) and no data; I read randomInsertionModelPhased.py, whose last line reads three files that are NOT in the deposit ('PA-1_insertions_phased.txt', '10kbp_bin_annotation_phased.txt', 'L1_EN_motifs.hs1_noY.PA-1.phased.txt'). Queried the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) project PRJEB88944 ('Epigenomic analyses of L1 integration preferences in human cell lines'): 92 sequencing runs, 1,537.7 GB of FASTQ (raw read files) totalled from the ENA file report, 5 biological samples (PA-1_Faulkner, PA-1_Moran_2011, PA-1_Moran_2012, PD20F_Faulkner, PD20F_D2_Faulkner), with zero 'analysis' (processed-file) objects. The companion project PRJEB109977 (nanopore sequencing of PA-1 and H9 cells for haplotype single-nucleotide polymorphism calling) returns an empty run list. Searched Zenodo ('Rios Barreda' -> 1 record, the code; 'L1 integration' -> 2 records), GitHub (0 repositories), NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus and BioProject (no matching processed deposit). The Science article page returned HTTP 403 Forbidden to both the fetch helper and the web fetcher, and the paper is not in PubMed Central, so the supplementary tables could not be opened.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything scientific: that roughly 30,000 engineered L1 (long interspersed element-1, a 'jumping gene') insertions were mapped, that integration favoured the inactive X chromosome, and that late-replicating regions were preferred. The abstract plus a press release are all I could read; no methods, no data-availability statement, no row counts, no column definitions, no units were ever seen.

a1_downloadable.note: The raw reads are public (ENA PRJEB88944, no login), but the table an ML project needs - phased insertion coordinates and per-window haplotype annotations - is deposited nowhere: Zenodo has code only (verified by listing files), ENA has no processed-file objects (verified, empty analysis report), and the Science supplement is paywalled (HTTP 403 on two independent fetchers).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label (did an engineered L1 insert at this site, and on which of the two chromosome haplotypes) exists only as a file named in the authors' script that they did not deposit; building it means calling insertions from 1.5 TB of long reads and phasing them to maternal/paternal copies.

a3_inputs_present.note: The features - DNA methylation, H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 histone marks, Repli-Seq replication timing, Iso-Seq transcription, per 10 kb window per haplotype - are only present as raw FASTQ reads; every track would have to be aligned, phased and quantified from scratch.

a4_units_stated.note: Cannot be checked: no data file was obtainable. The script reads nine unnamed numeric columns per haplotype with no header beyond 'seg_id', so units are implied rather than stated even in the code.

a5_enough_rows.note: A press release states nearly 30,000 L1 insertions were characterised, which would comfortably exceed the 1,500-row bar - but I verified no row count in any file, so n_rows is null.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 1,537.7 GB of FASTQ across 92 runs (verified from the ENA file report), including a single 86.2 GB nanopore whole-genome run
a6_fits_laptop.note: Rebuilding the feature/label table needs long-read alignment to the T2T-CHM13 (hs1) genome, haplotype phasing and methylation calling - a cluster job, not a 16 GB laptop, and the project rules forbid downloading raw sequencing data at all.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Unverifiable: there is no downloadable table whose rows could be counted against the paper's claim.

a8_label_provenance.note: The label is a physical measurement - an engineered L1 reporter that actually integrated, detected by targeted long-read sequencing - not another model's output, so there is no circularity. This is the one Part A item the study clearly satisfies.

existing_models.name: DeepHINT (deep learning model for HIV-1 integration site prediction, Bioinformatics 2019)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to predict HIV-1 integration sites from genomic sequence with attention weights linking to Pol II binding (4.5-fold enrichment) and DNase hypersensitivity (1.9-fold); exact metric and split not retrieved beyond the abstract.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - only the abstract and a review summary were read.

existing_models.name: Sleeping Beauty transposon insertion-site predictors (support vector machine and artificial neural network, Springer 2014)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported that the support vector machine outperformed the neural network at recognising preferred insertion regions; no numbers or split retrieved.

existing_models.name: Flasch et al. / Sultana et al. style statistical models of L1 pre-insertion sequence bias (Molecular Cell 2019 and Cell 2019)
existing_models.score_and_split: Descriptive enrichment analyses rather than a trained predictor; they report L1 targeting the L1 endonuclease motif genome-wide with a bias for early-replicating domains, which this paper's haplotype-aware result contradicts for the inactive X.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Whether chromatin state causes targeting, as opposed to correlating with it - the question this paper addresses.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 (DNA language models with open weights) would be the natural fit for sequence features around an insertion site
backbone.hardware: CPU-feasible for a few tens of thousands of short windows if the label table existed
backbone.licence: Open weights; not evaluated further because the data failed Part A

integration.partner_dataset: 4D Nucleome / ENCODE replication-timing and histone-mark tracks, and the T2T-CHM13 (hs1) reference annotation, joinable on genomic coordinates
integration.join_key: genomic coordinates plus genome build (hs1 / T2T-CHM13)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does the epigenetic state of a chromosome copy, rather than its DNA sequence, decide where new jumping-gene insertions land - and does that explain why the X chromosome carries so many of them?

controls.positive_control: The paper's own Monte Carlo null model: a working pipeline must recover the known enrichment of insertions at the L1 endonuclease consensus motif, and the reported preference for late-replicating regions.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the haplotype assignment of each insertion between the active and inactive X; the inactive-X preference must vanish.
controls.external_validation: The PD20F fibroblast samples in the same ENA project are a second cell background, and published L1 insertion maps from HeLa and HEK293 exist - but none of these is available as a processed table either.

honest_claim_h3: If the insertion table existed, a model could claim only: within one teratocarcinoma cell line engineered to over-express an L1 reporter, the haplotype-resolved epigenetic state of a 10 kb window predicts whether an L1 lands there - a statement about engineered insertions in a cancer cell line, not about natural germline mutation.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the local epigenetic state of each chromosome copy to predict where a jumping gene will insert itself.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be a 10 kb stretch of one chromosome copy described by DNA methylation, two histone marks, replication timing and transcription; the paper implies roughly 30,000 insertion events, but I verified no count because no data table is public.
plain_idea.predict: Whether an engineered L1 (long interspersed element-1, a mobile DNA element) inserted at that site and on which chromosome copy; the true answer comes from targeted long-read DNA sequencing of the cells after the reporter jumped.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Clinical geneticists would learn whether new disease-causing insertions are drawn to the silenced X chromosome, which would change how X-linked disease risk is estimated in families; even a failure would show that epigenetic state alone does not pick insertion sites.

more_or_better_data.why: Haplotype-resolved insertion data separating the active from the inactive X is genuinely new - no existing model had it - but I could not verify a single row of it, and published L1 maps from HeLa and HEK293 cells are larger and already public as tables.

confidence_score.why: Without the insertion table or any replicate-level file I cannot tell whether the data supports per-site uncertainty; the only deposited material is raw reads and three analysis scripts.

models_beatable.why: The nearest predictors are a 2014 support vector machine on Sleeping Beauty transposons and the 2019 DeepHINT model for HIV-1, neither built for L1 nor for haplotype-resolved features, so they would be beatable - but there is no shared split or shared data to beat them on.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition outright: there is no accessible feature/label table, so neither our model nor any baseline can be run at all.

ml_idea: Predict, per haplotype-resolved 10 kb genomic window, whether an engineered L1 reporter integrated there, from DNA methylation, H3K4me3, H3K27me3, replication timing and transcription, with the active versus inactive X chromosome as a built-in internal contrast (same DNA sequence, opposite epigenetic state) - a near-ideal natural experiment that is unusable because the insertion coordinates and annotation windows were never deposited.

effort.compute_note: Working set is the verified total of 1,537.7 GB of FASTQ across 92 ENA runs; no laptop estimate is meaningful because the feature/label table would first have to be rebuilt by long-read alignment, haplotype phasing and methylation calling on a cluster. Nothing was timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: List the files in the Zenodo deposit and the ENA analysis objects - two API calls, two minutes: the three input files named in the authors' own script are in neither, which kills the project.

verdict_reason: The scientifically beautiful part - the same DNA sequence in two opposite epigenetic states, giving a built-in controlled comparison for where jumping genes land - is exactly the part that was never deposited. The authors released three Python scripts whose final line reads 'PA-1_insertions_phased.txt', '10kbp_bin_annotation_phased.txt' and 'L1_EN_motifs.hs1_noY.PA-1.phased.txt', and none of those three files is in the Zenodo record, in ENA, in GEO, or anywhere else I could find; the Science supplement that might hold them is paywalled and returns HTTP 403. What is public is 1,537.7 GB of raw reads from five samples, which fails A6 on size and is forbidden by the project's own no-raw-sequencing rule. A1, A2, A3, A4, A6 and A7 all fail; only A8 (the label is a real measurement, not a model's output) passes cleanly. Worth re-checking in roughly six months if the paper enters PubMed Central or the authors add the three tables to Zenodo - at that point it would be a strong candidate, because the active-versus-inactive-X contrast is a positive control most genomics datasets lack.
